Time Lapse by @salvarezphoto (Stephen Alvarez)
We had tried to do something stupid, climb an unknown mountain covered with fresh snow by moonlight. Slogging up through thigh deep snow @BurchamPhoto and I took turns breaking trail. We’d just cleared tree line, me in the lead, when the entire snow field settled with a distinctive “whoomph.” Even as a flatlander I knew that was a bad sound, the sign of unstable snow. No avalanche probes, no shovel, no one who knew where we were. A quick conference and we beat a hasty retreat, properly chastised by the mountains. Then crossing the valley we were handed the most wonderful gift. A brief but beautiful Aurora display that we would have completely missed had we still been on the mountain…
Shot on a #lumia950 smartphone
See more of our travels in the far north chasing the Aurora at @LumiaxNatgeo

Photo by @EdKashi  Workers tend to cannabis plants at the Medicine Man marijuana grow house in Denver, Colorado. Colorado lead the United States into uncharted territory by legalizing marijuana sales as of January 1, 2014. Even before the new law came into effect, burglaries and break-ins at medical pot dispensaries and grow houses were an issue, and since the law was passed the problem has significantly worsened. This is a result of the lack of coordination between state and federal banking laws, which makes these legal businesses unable to deposit their cash in a bank, leaving them exposed as easy targets for robbery. Interestingly, a new crop of private security firms have also sprouted in the state, often run and staffed by former United States military personnel, including former special ops soldiers, which leads to the interesting situation where former members of the military are guarding the legalized marijuana industry. @viiphoto

The Wallcreeper lives in a hostile, mostly inhospitable environment of high-mountain cliff faces, some more than 16,000 feet high.  Some insects and reptiles have flourished in this environment of few predators.  The Wallcreeper evolved to take advantage of this habitat, developing extremely sharp claws and tough, broad feathers in their wings to push off against rock faces from their minuscule holds, bounding along the cliffs in short, powerful bursts.

This image was originally taken on an assignment for @natgeo for an article, The Curious Evolution of Feathers.  The subsequent collection of images taken for that assignment have been compiled into a book: Feathers - Displays of Brilliant Plumage.

Check out @RobertClarkPhoto for more feathers and information regarding the book.

Photo by @stevemccurryofficial // Isolation and bitter winters define the central highland's villages like Qala-e Sabzi in the Koh-i-Baba mountains, an extension of the Hindu Kush mountains in Afghanistan. The harsh land is integral to this nomadic herder culture with deep roots in high pastures. It is the wild, stubborn and unconquerable spirit of this ancient country that has drawn me back again and again for thirty-five years. 
Starting March 5, experience Afghanistan’s unique culture and beauty in the @turquoisemountain exhibition at Freer Sackler, the Smithsonian’s museum of Asian art, in Washington, D.C.

Usman wears numerous clothes pins as a sign of loosing a card game called song, a popular pass time on the island of Sungsang off the east coast of Sumatra, Indonesia, in the Banka Straits.

The third story I did for @NatGeo was on the Malacca Straits. I spent two days on Sungsang, a lovely and welcoming island off the coast of Sumatra situated along the western edge of the infamous strait. There I met Mr. Usman, significantly loosing in a card game called Song — the more points one looses, the more clothing pins one clips to their face. In this match, Usman was clearly showing the predicament he was in.

Photograph by George Steinmetz @geosteinmetz/@thephotosociety Lake Vanda in Wright Valley has what is said to be the clearest ice in the world. The lake water is almost completely chlorophyl and sediment free, and transports light only 10% less than distilled water.  While walking across the ice I could see the bottom through solid ice some 7 meters below as if I was looking through a glass-top table. At the lake center the bottom is 65m down and the bottom water is hyper saline. This salty (10x saltier than sea water) layer traps heat and keeps the bottom water and 25°C year-round, and supports lots of bacteria which live off the incoming sunlight. To see more photos from Antarctica visit @geosteinmetz
